Shift & Spectrum · Discovery mock-up

Discovery hunts

Discovery stays as it is: open it, pick a patch of sky, then choose what to look for. Ten hunts, sorted by how likely an ordinary person is to make a credited find. Each uses the data that can actually see its kind of object, shows the evidence and detection rate behind every lead, and sends finds to the project that can credit you.

How it finds it

Period searches on every light curve (Lomb–Scargle for pulsing, box search for eclipses), then a small classifier trained on stars already in the AAVSO index.

When it counts as a candidate

The same period in two independent data sets (TESS and ZTF), and no match in VSX, ASAS-SN or Gaia's variable list. Unsure shapes go to your eye, not to the classifier.

Where it goes

Prepare for VSX: one star at a time, moderated, under your own account. Every row also exports in the research bundle.

How it finds it

Stars that move year over year in WISE (2010 to 2024), are very red and too faint for Gaia. SPHEREx's 102 colours then test for methane, the mark of a cold atmosphere.

When it counts as a candidate

Motion measured at 5σ or more, the right colour, a methane dip, and no match in SIMBAD. Type, temperature and distance are model estimates.

Where it goes

Prepare for Backyard Worlds' public form, or export the bundle. Types come from SPHEREx only to about T6; colder ones say so.

How it finds it

Searches TESS light curves for repeating dips, and keeps single and odd-shaped dips the pipelines discard.

When it counts as a candidate

Three dips or more with the standard checks passed, or one clean dip flagged as a possible long-period planet. Crowding is flagged, not hidden.

Where it goes

Release 2. ExoFOP now takes only published candidates, so the route is an RNAAS note from the exported bundle.

How it finds it

Predicts where each known asteroid was in archive images, cuts out and stacks them, then compares its fuzziness with stars of the same brightness.

When it counts as a candidate

Wider than a star in more than one image, with any tail pointing away from the Sun, and no activity on record.

Where it goes

Release 2. Export the images and profiles for a research note; astrometry to the MPC under your own program code.

How it finds it

Reads public ZTF alerts through a broker (ALeRCE, Fink or Lasair) and keeps those inside the patch, with the broker's classification.

When it counts as a candidate

A brightening of 1 mag or more on two nights, with no match in the Transient Name Server or the variable-star index.

Where it goes

Context only: the surveys report these within hours, and Galactic novae go to CBAT, not TNS. Shown to sit beside other hunts' rows.

How it finds it

Turns Gaia motions and distances into speeds across the sky, and flags stars far faster than their neighbours. Their paths are traced back through the Galaxy.

When it counts as a candidate

A good parallax (better than 10%), a speed well above the local spread, and no match in runaway-star lists. Speed towards us is shown as not measured when Gaia has none.

Where it goes

An RNAAS research note from the exported bundle. Experimental until its control is measured: known runaways only.

How it finds it

Fits a star model to Gaia and 2MASS, then compares WISE and SPHEREx: a star much brighter than the model in infrared has warm dust around it, or something odd.

When it counts as a candidate

Excess in two WISE bands, no Gaia neighbour, a point-like image and no 3.3 µm galaxy feature in SPHEREx. Most leads still turn out to be blends.

Where it goes

Characterisation: SPHEREx spectra of WISE excess stars, with the 3.3 µm galaxy test. Export for a research note.

This is the real app

The finished overnight run of 14 November (a different patch, near RA 223° Dec +11°), captured as it is today: 35 known, 0 found, 83 unexplained.

What changes here

  • The hunt switch appears at the top of this card.
  • A square with missing star lists is skipped, not completed.
  • Known rocks get a "What it's made of" spectrum.

What it returns now

Known rocks measured along their paths, with spectra and precovery. Blind tracks stay "possible" until they have 2 nights, 3 tracklets and an orbit fit. ADES to the MPC once SPHEREx has an observatory code.

5How the hunts work

Architecture for the build · research checked 17 Nov 2026 · sizes and times are first estimates

All hunts run on the user's own computer, inside the existing local backend; the browser only displays results. For each hunt we chose the most accurate published method, then the lightest version of it that still fits a gaming PC. Each hunt has the same four parts: the data we take from the satellite, what we study in it, how we process it and what comes out.

Revised 18 November 2026

  • A research tool: every hunt returns a table with provenance, completeness and purity against expected signal-to-noise, a selection function and a reproducibility bundle. Credit routes are replaced by export, and by "Prepare a submission" only for VSX, Backyard Worlds, RNAAS drafts and (later) the MPC.
  • Re-scoped: lenses removed; novae a context layer; black holes a cross-match with Gaia DR4's own table; infrared excess becomes SPHEREx characterisation; asteroids become "known rocks" first, with blind tracks needing 2 nights, 3 tracklets and an orbit fit. New in release 2: slow movers in TESS stares.
  • The sheets below are the first draft's summary for a general reader. Where they differ, the spec (docs/architecture/discovery-hunts.md) wins.

From the satellite to your card

Seven steps every hunt follows

  1. Check coverageAsk each archive what covers each square. A square without the input a hunt needs is marked skipped, never treated as empty.
  2. Catalogues firstStar lists and known-object lists are megabytes, and cut most of the work before any image is fetched.
  3. Pixels only where neededCutouts, not whole images; ranged reads from the public cloud copies.
  4. DetectThe hunt's own method, set out in its sheet below.
  5. VetPhysics checks and a match against everything already known. Anything that fails is labelled with the reason.
  6. CalibrateEach hunt version ships with a detection-rate table, measured by injecting fake objects into real data. The card reads the rate for the lead's brightness.
  7. ReportEvery value carries its provenance. Leads export in the format of the body that can credit them.

Rules carried over from the app

  • Refuse rather than invent: a missing input fails the square, with the reason shown.
  • Data first: every physical number comes from code, never from a language model.
  • Leads, not discoveries: the app never says "discovered".
  • Known objects are shown as recoveries. Recovering them is how each hunt proves it works, and it is the learning moment for students.

How to read the sheets

  • Most accurate is the best published method. At home is what we run on a gaming PC, and what it costs in accuracy.
  • Accuracy figures are from the cited papers, not from our code. Ours will be measured by injection before launch.
  • (to verify) marks a figure seen only in a secondary source or a preprint.

Good chance

Variable and eclipsing stars

Stars that pulse, or pairs that eclipse each other, repeat a pattern. The hunt finds the period hidden in a few hundred uneven measurements and checks that nobody has catalogued it yet.

1 · Data in

  • ZTF data release light curves (DR24): g, r and i brightness, tens to over 1,000 nights per star. IRSA light-curve API by cone, or the AWS Parquet copy.
  • TESS light curves where the patch has them: dense but blurred (21″ pixels), so used to confirm periods, not to find faint stars.
  • Gaia DR3 variability tables (10.5 million variables) and parallaxes, via TAP.
  • Known lists to cross-match: AAVSO VSX, Chen et al. 2020 ZTF periodic catalogue (781,602 stars, downloadable), Gaia variables, ASAS-SN.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. CleanKeep good-quality points only (ZTF catalogue flags); require at least 30 to 40 nights.
  2. Is it variable?A variability index (Stetson J, reduced χ²) over all stars. Only the variable few per cent go further.
  3. Find the periodLomb–Scargle for smooth pulsations; a box search for sharp eclipses. Multi-band periodograms combine g and r.
  4. Alias checksReject 1-day and sidereal-day peaks; test half and double the period.
  5. TypeLight-curve features into a random-forest classifier trained on VSX stars, as ALeRCE does. Gaia parallax places the star on the colour–brightness diagram.
  6. Cross-matchVSX, Chen 2020, Gaia, ASAS-SN. A match is a recovery.
  7. ConfirmSame period in a second, independent data set (TESS or another ZTF band) before it becomes a lead.

4 · Output

  • Fields: position, IDs, nights used, period ± error, amplitude, suggested type with probability, alias flag, matches, folded-curve image, status (known / possibly new).
  • Expected accuracy: ALeRCE's classifier reaches 0.96 precision and 0.99 recall at the top level (periodic, stochastic, transient), but 0.57 and 0.76 for fine types. So the app shows the type as a suggestion.
  • Odds: bright, large-amplitude stars are almost all known. Real credit is in the leftovers: stars missing from VSX but varying in ZTF or Gaia, better types for stars listed only as "variable", and corrected periods.
  • Credit: VSX moderators check that a star is correctly identified, variable and new. They do not accept bulk automated submissions, so the app helps you submit one star at a time.

At home

  • A patch is 10⁴ to 10⁵ ZTF stars, tens to hundreds of MB (to measure).
  • The variability cut leaves a few thousand; periodograms for those run in minutes on CPU, faster batched on the GPU.

Sources: Chen et al. 2020 · Sánchez-Sáez et al. 2021 (ALeRCE) · Eyer et al. 2023 (Gaia DR3 variables) · ZTF light-curve API · VSX submissions

Good chance

Cold nearby worlds

The coldest brown dwarfs near the Sun are too faint to see in visible light, but they move across the sky year after year and glow at 4.6 µm. The census within 20 parsecs is complete except for exactly these: types T8 and colder, below 600 K.

1 · Data in

  • WISE / NEOWISE: CatWISE2020 (1.9 billion sources with motions, 2010 to 2018) via IRSA TAP; unTimely catalogue and time-resolved unWISE images (about 16 epochs per band to 2020) for movers too faint for catalogues.
  • 2MASS, VHS, UKIDSS, Pan-STARRS, Legacy Surveys for the near-infrared and visible: a real Y dwarf is missing in most of them.
  • Gaia DR3 to reject ordinary moving stars, and for wide companions.
  • SPHEREx spectral images (0.75 to 5 µm, 102 channels, 6.2″ pixels): forced photometry at the object's position in each frame.
  • Known lists: UltracoolSheet, the 20-pc census, Backyard Worlds lists, SIMBAD.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. Catalogue moversCatWISE sources with motion above 5σ and red W1 − W2, using its motion-corrected magnitudes. A patch drops from hundreds of thousands of rows to tens.
  2. Faint moversDifference first and last unWISE epochs: a mover leaves a bright–dark pair. A small network ranks the pairs; you check each in the flip-book.
  3. Reject impostorsCatalogue artefact flags, bright-star haloes, one-epoch artefacts, Gaia stars with normal colours.
  4. Long baselineMatch 2MASS, WISE and VHS positions for up to 25 years of motion; reduced proper motion separates nearby dwarfs from distant stars.
  5. SpectrumForced photometry in SPHEREx frames at the position for each frame's date (fast movers shift by a large part of a pixel per year).
  6. TypeFit spectral templates per subtype (the 2026 SPHEREx ultracool-dwarf library) and model atmospheres (Sonora, ATMO) on the GPU.
  7. DistanceParallax where measured; otherwise from type and brightness, marked Estimated.

4 · Output

  • Fields: position at epoch, motion ± error, W1 and W2 (or W1 limit), W1 − W2, reduced proper motion, Gaia match, SPHEREx bands used, best template and χ², type range, distance with its provenance, and a "missing" list.
  • Expected accuracy: CatWISE motions agree with Gaia to about 20 mas/yr at W1 ≈ 15 and 100 mas/yr at W1 ≈ 17. Spitzer colours remain the best cheap typing for Y dwarfs (17 of 170 CatWISE candidates were Y-like). SPHEREx typing accuracy is not yet published (to verify).
  • Odds: Backyard Worlds volunteers had found more than 1,500 brown dwarfs by 2020 (to verify); the coldest, faintest ones are still missing, and that is where motion-only methods are needed.
  • Credit: Backyard Worlds, whose volunteers co-author the papers.

At home

  • CatWISE averages about 46,000 sources per square degree: tens of MB for a patch.
  • Images are fetched only for the survivors; template fits are one matrix product on the GPU.

Sources: Marocco et al. 2021 (CatWISE2020) · Meisner et al. 2023 (unTimely) · Kirkpatrick et al. 2021 (20-pc census) · Marocco et al. 2020 · SPHEREx ultracool-dwarf library (preprint) · Bock et al. (SPHEREx mission)

Good chance

Strange dimmers and planets

A planet crossing its star dims it by a small, regular amount. The TESS pipelines find most repeating dips. People still win on the leftovers: a single dip from a long-period planet, and odd shapes such as exocomets and disintegrating planets.

1 · Data in

  • TESS light curves from MAST (or the AWS copy): SPOC 2-minute and 20-second, TESS-SPOC and QLP from full-frame images, TGLC for crowded fields.
  • TESScut pixel cutouts, for candidates only, to see where the dip comes from.
  • TESS Input Catalog (star size, temperature, light from neighbours) and Gaia DR3 neighbours.
  • Kepler / K2 where they overlap; the TOI list, ExoFOP and the NASA Exoplanet Archive for known planets.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. Choose starsBright enough (about TESS mag 13.5) for a small planet's dip to show, and not swamped by neighbours. The cut is shown on the card.
  2. DetrendTukey biweight sliding filter (wotan): the most robust choice in its benchmark; a box filter loses about 5 to 10% of small planets.
  3. SearchBox Least Squares on the GPU for all stars; Transit Least Squares only where the box search's signal is strong (SDE ≥ 6).
  4. Single dipsA separate search for lone dips, fitted with a transit model; these are kept, not discarded.
  5. Odd shapesAsymmetric dips (exocomets), changing depths (disintegrating planets) and irregular dips (dipper stars) are flagged for you to look at.
  6. VetOdd–even depths, secondary eclipse, centroid shift in TESScut pixels, Gaia neighbours, momentum-dump and scattered-light flags; a false-positive probability (TRICERATOPS).
  7. MatchTOI list and Exoplanet Archive; a match is a recovery.

4 · Output

  • Fields: TIC ID, sectors, mid-time, depth (ppm), duration (h), period or "single", signal strength, odd–even difference, centroid offset, vetting flags, planet size (Estimated, from the star's size).
  • Expected accuracy: Transit Least Squares recovers 93% of injected small planets against 76% for a box search, at a 1% false-alarm rate. It takes about 10 s per long light curve on a laptop.
  • Odds: Planet Hunters TESS reported 90 strong new candidates from the first two years, 73 of them single transits. That niche is still open.
  • Credit: Planet Hunters TESS and ExoFOP.

At home

  • Light curves, never full-frame images: gigabytes per patch, not terabytes.
  • Stars × trial periods in one GPU kernel; TLS on the top few per cent across CPU cores.

Sources: Hippke & Heller 2019 (TLS) · Hippke et al. 2019 (wotan) · Eisner et al. (Planet Hunters TESS II) · TOI-813 b

Good chance

Asteroids, precovery and what rocks are made of

The first SPHEREx run found 0 of 38 known asteroids. The likely reason: SPHEREx records each spot at a different, narrow wavelength, so a rock is much fainter in any one frame than its usual brightness suggests. The fix is to start from known orbits, and to stack frames for unknowns.

1 · Data in

  • SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images (about 70 MB each, one per detector, 6 per pointing; 6.15″ pixels) with flags, variance and PSF layers. IRSA cutout service or the AWS copy. Use the spectral-WCS product for wavelengths, not the visual lookup table.
  • Release: IRSA lists DR1 as released this month, replacing QR2 (to verify); frames pulled before April 2026 need re-pulling for corrected PSFs.
  • ZTF, DECam, Pan-STARRS archive images for deeper visible-light checks.
  • Orbits: MPC orbit file, JPL Horizons and SkyBoT for where each known rock should be at each frame's time; NEOWISE for sizes.
  • Gaia DR3 and CatWISE for star masks and astrometric calibration.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. Predict firstPosition and expected brightness of every known rock in each frame, at that frame's wavelength. Rocks below the frame's limit are listed as "too faint here", not as misses. This is the first test of the likely cause of the 0 of 38.
  2. Forced photometryMeasure at the predicted spot with the frame's own PSF, frame by frame.
  3. Remove the fixed skySubtract a template of the static sky built from other frames at the same wavelength; mask Gaia and CatWISE stars (required, or the square fails).
  4. Search for unknownsCatalogue-based shift-and-stack over a grid of motions (10 to 1,000× faster than image stacking, about 0.25 mag shallower); image stacking (KBMOD) on the GPU only for the deep fields near the ecliptic poles.
  5. ConfirmAbove 5σ in the stack, seen in both halves of the frames, with the frame's star shape; no known orbit explains it.
  6. Spectra of known rocksJoin the per-frame measurements into a 0.75 to 5 µm spectrum; remove heat emission (NEATM) and spin brightness changes, which can mimic spectral features; compare with Bus–DeMeo classes and measure the 3 µm water band.
  7. PrecoveryRun a known object's orbit and uncertainty back to every archived frame; search inside the uncertainty area, stacking along the path if faint.

4 · Output

  • Fields: designation or temporary ID, mid-exposure time (UTC), position ± error, magnitude and band, channel wavelength, flux ± error, frame flags.
  • Expected accuracy: stacking N frames gains 2.5 log √N magnitudes. No published accuracy yet for SPHEREx asteroid spectra; the team expects about 100,000 asteroids with useful flux (to verify).
  • Gate: the hunt must recover the known rocks predicted above its limit before it shows any new lead.
  • Credit: ADES to the Minor Planet Center. Since August 2025 measurements from archive images need a program code and checking by the MPC's archive team first (to verify the process).

At home

  • Cutouts processed in 512-pixel tiles, deleted after each square unless kept.
  • GPU for sky subtraction, stacking and batched forced photometry; downloads remain the bottleneck (about 36 minutes a square on 14 Nov).

Sources: SPHEREx data products · IRSA SPHEREx releases · Whidden et al. 2019 (KBMOD) · Catalogue shift-and-stack (preprint) · Holman et al. 2018 (HelioLinC) · MPC archive submissions

Good chance

Active asteroids

A few asteroids grow a faint tail or haze, from ice, collisions or spinning apart. Fewer than about 60 are known among more than a million asteroids (to verify). The activity is often brief and hides in archive images nobody re-examined.

1 · Data in

  • DECam archive images (NOIRLab Astro Data Archive): deep, the source the Active Asteroids project uses.
  • ZTF images (IRSA) for more nights, less depth; SPHEREx frames for the infrared.
  • Orbits from the MPC, and the Sun and orbit directions at each image's time from JPL Horizons.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. PredictPositions of every known asteroid in the patch at each archive image time.
  2. Cut outSmall cutouts centred on the prediction; skip images where it is too faint or on a bright star.
  3. Compare profilesAsteroid profile against stars of the same brightness in the same image (the SAFARI method); score the excess in the wings.
  4. Tail directionMeasure the angle of any extension; compare with the anti-Sun and behind-the-orbit angles.
  5. RejectBackground galaxies, blended stars, cosmic rays, ghosts, trailing from the asteroid's own motion.
  6. You decideThe images are shown side by side; nothing is sent without your yes.

4 · Output

  • Fields: designation, image times, cutout IDs, profile excess, tail angle, anti-Sun and behind-orbit angles, your grade.
  • Expected rate: the Active Asteroids project (8,300 volunteers, 430,000 cutouts) found 15 asteroids and a Centaur with new activity. Finds are rare; one patch will usually give none.
  • Credit: Active Asteroids on Zooniverse, then the MPC.

At home

  • Cutouts only, a few hundred KB each; profile fits run on the CPU.

Sources: Chandler et al. 2024 (Active Asteroids) · Chandler et al. 2018 (SAFARI)

Possible

Novae and supernovae

A star that suddenly brightens. Surveys and their alert brokers report most of these to the Transient Name Server within minutes, so this hunt reads their alerts rather than repeating their work, and looks for what automated cuts drop.

1 · Data in

  • Rubin public alerts (live since 24 February 2026) and ZTF alerts, through brokers: ALeRCE, Fink, Lasair, ANTARES. A cone query on the patch, kilobytes to a few MB.
  • ZTF and ATLAS forced photometry for the history at that spot.
  • Legacy Surveys, Pan-STARRS for the host galaxy; Gaia for stars.
  • Known: the TNS object list, VSX, SIMBAD.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. FetchBroker alerts inside the patch; group them by object.
  2. FilterReal/bogus score above threshold, at least two detections; remove asteroids, known variables, active galaxy nuclei and stars.
  3. HistoryForced photometry: was it there before? Earlier detections are a precovery, useful to TNS.
  4. ClassifyA small light-curve classifier (SuperNNova or ParSNIP) runs locally next to the broker's class.
  5. HostOffset from the nearest galaxy; faint or far-offset hosts are the cases automated cuts often miss.
  6. WatchSaved objects are rechecked daily.

4 · Output

  • Fields: position, first detection, peak brightness, rise and decline, host and offset, broker and local class with probability, real/bogus score, matches, image stamps.
  • Expected accuracy: SuperNNova separates Type Ia from other supernovae with about 97% accuracy on full simulated light curves; real data does worse. ParSNIP reached 82% on 472 confirmed supernovae (to verify).
  • Odds: a first report on a bright new event is unlikely. Earlier detections, odd hosts and late reclassification are where users add something.
  • Credit: TNS; the card warns that surveys usually report first.

At home

  • No image processing at all: the surveys did it. Minutes per patch.

Sources: Rubin alerts and brokers · Möller & de Boissière 2020 (SuperNNova) · Boone 2021 (ParSNIP)

Possible

Runaway stars

Some stars are flung out of their birth cluster by a supernova or a close encounter, and move far faster than their neighbours. Gaia measures their motion; tracing the path back shows where they came from.

1 · Data in

  • Gaia DR3 positions, motions, parallaxes and quality flags, via TAP for the patch.
  • Bailer-Jones distances (in the Gaia archive).
  • Gaia radial velocities where they exist (brighter stars only). Many fast candidates have none, shown as "not measured".
  • Cluster catalogues and known runaway and hypervelocity lists.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. Quality cutRUWE below 1.4 (some use 1.25), parallax better than 10%, no excess astrometric noise.
  2. CorrectApply Gaia's parallax zero-point correction (Lindegren et al.); use Bayesian distances, not 1/parallax.
  3. SpeedVelocity across the sky, with Monte Carlo errors; flag stars far outside the local spread.
  4. Trace backIntegrate a few hundred random draws per star back through a Galaxy model (galpy) for the fastest few only.
  5. OriginClosest approach to known clusters, the Galactic centre and the Large Magellanic Cloud.
  6. RejectBad astrometry, crowded-field blends, spurious radial velocities.

4 · Output

  • Fields: Gaia ID, parallax and its quality, distance with range, speed across the sky, radial velocity or "not measured", probability of being unbound, best origin and closest approach.
  • Reality check: among 34 million Gaia stars with full 3D speeds, no star fast enough to leave the Galaxy was found. Most leads will be ordinary runaways, still useful for a research note.
  • Credit: a research note; candidates without radial velocity need a spectrum from a professional telescope.

At home

  • Catalogue only, under 0.2 GB a patch; orbit integration runs on the CPU in minutes.

Sources: Marchetti 2022 (Gaia DR3 fast stars) · Brown et al. 2018 · Search without radial velocities (2025)

Possible

Infrared excess

A star with a disk of warm dust glows more at long wavelengths than the star alone can. Most such excesses turn out to be something else, a background galaxy or a blend, so this hunt is mostly about ruling those out.

1 · Data in

  • WISE: AllWISE at 3.4, 4.6, 12 and 22 µm, with quality flags; unWISE images for the visual check.
  • 2MASS and Gaia DR3 for the star itself (brightness, temperature, distance, RUWE, neighbours).
  • SPHEREx spectra from 0.75 to 5 µm: pin down the star and any hot dust; they cannot see cold dust, and their 6.2″ pixels do not separate blends.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. Clean starsGaia match, RUWE below 1.4, reliable WISE signal (W4 signal-to-noise above 3).
  2. Star modelFit a model atmosphere to Gaia, 2MASS and SPHEREx points, temperature from Gaia.
  3. Excessχ = (measured − model) / error at W3 and W4, using precise WISE calibration; flag χ above 3.
  4. Rule outPhotocentre shift between WISE bands (a galaxy beside the star), Gaia neighbours inside the beam, nebulosity and artefact flags, extended shape.
  5. DustFit a single blackbody to the excess for temperature and fractional brightness (Model-dependent).
  6. You inspectunWISE cutouts in every band, as Disk Detective volunteers do.

4 · Output

  • Fields: Gaia ID, distance, temperature, WISE magnitudes with flags, model prediction, χ per band, dust temperature and fraction, blend flag and nearest neighbour, your verdict.
  • Expected accuracy: at most 7.9% of WISE-selected excesses are good disk candidates; earlier searches without image checks had over 70% false positives. The card says so.
  • Credit: Disk Detective, whose volunteers co-author papers. The app never suggests exotic explanations.

At home

  • Catalogues plus a few cutouts per candidate; model fits on the CPU in minutes.

Sources: Silverberg et al. 2018 · Kuchner et al. 2016 (Disk Detective) · Cotten & Song 2016 · Faintest WISE debris disks

Possible

Sleeping black holes

A star orbiting an unseen, heavy partner wobbles. Gaia found three black holes this way (BH1 to BH3; BH3 is 33 times the Sun's mass). Gaia DR4, due 2 December 2026, publishes the raw position measurements for the first time.

1 · Data in

  • Gaia DR4 (66 months of data): epoch astrometry (62 TB in all, so queried per patch, never downloaded whole), about 5.9 million two-body orbit solutions, and radial velocities.
  • Gaia DR3 orbit solutions now, for building and testing.
  • Known black holes, neutron stars and spurious solutions from the literature.

2 · What we study

3 · Processing

  1. Read Gaia's orbitsTwo-body solutions in the patch, with their significance.
  2. MassStar's mass from its temperature and brightness; partner's minimum mass from the mass function.
  3. Is it dark?A normal star of that mass would show up in the light and the spectrum; if it does not, the partner is compact.
  4. RefitFor high-mass candidates only, refit the orbit from the epoch positions (the same Thiele–Innes method Gaia uses).
  5. RejectSpurious solutions, hidden triples, white-dwarf partners, low radial-velocity agreement.

4 · Output

  • Fields: Gaia ID, period, eccentricity, orbit size, star mass and its source, partner minimum mass with range, RUWE, radial-velocity check, status (candidate, spurious, known).
  • Reality check: in one study of Gaia DR3 orbits, every candidate partner above 3 Suns proved spurious on spectroscopic follow-up. No lead is called a black hole before that.
  • Credit: a ranked candidate list for follow-up observers; confirmation needs large telescopes.

At home

  • Patch queries only; orbit refits for a handful of stars run on the CPU. Sizes to measure after 2 December.

Sources: ESA Gaia DR4 · Panuzzo et al. 2024 (Gaia BH3) · Review of Gaia compact-object binaries · Müller-Horn et al. 2026

Kept for learning, not discovery

  • Interstellar visitors: surveys catch them first; finding known ones in older SPHEREx frames is the useful part (asteroid sheet, precovery).
  • Planet X: stacking gives limits far more often than finds.
  • Ice along sightlines: SPHEREx's own speciality, a map rather than a discovery.
  • Microlensing and primordial black holes: surveys catch the events automatically, and no single event proves a primordial black hole.

Left out, on purpose

  • Galaxy distances for cosmology: SPHEREx's main goal, but it needs whole-sky statistics, not a patch.
  • Photographing planets next to their stars: not possible with these data.
  • Our own difference imaging for transients: the surveys do it better and faster.

First estimates, to be measured on a reference PC. Wall-clock time is set mostly by archive download speed, not by computation.

How it stays light

  1. Catalogues before pixelsMegabyte queries cut most work before any image is fetched.
  2. Cutouts and ranged readsRead only the needed part of each file from the AWS open-data copies (SPHEREx, TESS), with IRSA and MAST as fallback.
  3. Stream, don't hoardTiles in 32-bit floats; raw frames deleted when a square finishes unless kept; a disk budget evicts the oldest first.
  4. GPU where it paysShift-and-stack, FFT subtraction, batched BLS, model-grid fits and neural-network inference, through CuPy or PyTorch. A NumPy/Numba path gives the same results, and tests compare the two.
  5. Calibrated once, shippedInjection tests run once per hunt version and ship as tables, so home users never repeat them. Advanced users can re-measure.

Living with a gaming machine

  1. Resource managerOne GPU job at a time with a memory cap (for example 70%); a few download workers per archive, each with polite rate limits.
  2. Retries and mirrorsBack off and retry, then switch mirror. The 502 errors of 14 November failed 7 squares; a retry against the AWS copy might have saved them.
  3. CheckpointsPer square and per hunt (squares already do this), so a reboot resumes rather than restarts.
  4. Gaming modeLow priority; pauses when a game takes the GPU (read through NVML) or a laptop goes on battery; can be scheduled overnight.
  5. Share the workExport and import finished squares, so a class or astronomy club can split a big patch across several PCs and merge the results.

To check before building

  • SPHEREx DR1: exact date, DOI and product names on IRSA (one IRSA page lists it as released this month).
  • SPHEREx single-frame depth per channel, checked against the predicted brightness of the 38 rocks the first run missed.
  • The MPC's process and observatory code for measurements from archived space images.
  • Gaia DR4 epoch-data access per patch after 2 December, and its size.
  • Euclid DR1-Foundation access, and the published lens list to match against.
  • Rubin and ZTF broker query limits for a public tool.
  • How Backyard Worlds, Planet Hunters TESS, Active Asteroids and Disk Detective accept candidates found outside their own sites.
  • Accuracy of the vetting tools (TRICERATOPS and others) and of SPHEREx brown-dwarf typing, from the papers.
  • Every figure marked "to verify" in the hunt sheets.
  • Actual download sizes and run times for every hunt on a reference PC; ROCm support for consumer AMD cards.
